A-C002.description: According to Mrs. George S. Simpson (1904), the five builders and owners of the old Pueblo, at the mouth of Fountain Creek, were Robert Kinkaid, George S. Simpson, Francis Conn, Joseph Mantz (or Mantas), “French,” and a fifth man. Old Maurice LeDuc had worked for Kinkaid. The post was destroyed in the massacre carried out by the Utes on December 24, 1854.

A-C012.nom: Battle with the Blackfoot on the Salmon River (1832): Blackfoot, Nimíipuu, Salish
A-C012.description: In the spring of 1832, an American Fur Company brigade (35 men, captain “Weiser”) fights the Blackfoot on the Salmon River; Levanway loses an eye there, and Charles Nadeau also takes part. The brigade winters on the Salmon among the Nez Perce and the Flatheads. Autobees takes a Flathead wife there; Nadeau names their daughter Eliza.
A-C012.note: Approximate position on the Salmon River (Idaho).

A-C016.description: William Guerrier (“Bill Garey”), an independent trader among the Sioux near Fort Laramie, is killed when a spark from his pipe blows up a keg of powder in a tipi. His son Ed Guerrier, born of a Cheyenne mother, studied for seven years at a Catholic school in St. Louis and married Julia Bent.

A-C020.description: Joseph Levanway, whose real name was Barnois, is among the oldest trappers, having arrived before Autobees and Carson. A former North West Company man, he got lost in the Northwest with Portelance and two or three others and wintered among the Inuit, before reaching St. Louis and then joining the American Fur Company (1831). He dies in Walsenburg about three weeks after Charles Autobees (1882).

A-C026.description: In Denver, on August 22, 1908, Mrs. Mary L. Sopris states that she was born at Fort St. Vrain, in 1848 by her account (1846 according to her brother). Her mother, “Red,” a Sioux woman (perhaps a sister of Red Cloud), was the wife of Marcellin St. Vrain, Céran's brother. Marcellin returned to Missouri in the spring of 1848; his son Felix died of smallpox at Vicksburg during the Civil War.

A-C031.nom: Distribution of annuity goods on the Platte, below Fort Laramie (1858): Indigenous
A-C031.description: In the summer of 1858, another distribution takes place on the Platte below Fort Laramie. The wagons are drawn up in a circle, wheels chained together, and the goods divided into five shares for the tribes. Labrie notes the cleanliness of the Indians, who washed and combed their hair before meals.

A-C033.description: The Rocky Mountain News of 1859 reports a conference at the Blake and Williams hotel in Auraria with Little Raven, chief of the Arapaho; “Chat Dubray” serves as interpreter. Dubray, a Canadien trapper, had gone up the Missouri with Charles Autobees in 1828.

A-C035.description: In September 1902, Cragin visits the area around Whiterocks and draws a plan of “Old Ft. Robidoux.” According to the tradition gathered from L. W. Curry, the Robidoux party wanted both to trade with the Utes and to trap on its own; the Utes objected and the fort was abandoned. Auguste Archambeau later had a trading store near the old fort.

A-C037.nom: Battle of Battle Creek (Fraeb's fort, 1841): Arapaho, Sioux, Cheyenne
A-C037.description: A man named Sorel, brother of the Sorel who died at Fort Hall, was killed on Savory's Fork (Battle Creek) in a three-day fight between whites and Arapaho, Sioux and Cheyenne. There were 80 or 90 whites, Delawares and French at Fraeb's fort, including Jim Baker.

A-C038.description: Sorel, a stocky, fair-haired trapper, dies around 1894 at Fort Hall; his son Narcisse lives in Pocatello. A Métis daughter of Sorel and a Shoshone woman, Deliat, married Big Tom at Whiterocks.

A-C039.description: An informant of 1902 knew at the Pine Ridge agency Amos LaBonta, an old mountaineer who had come from Wyoming by the Chugwater, as well as Nicholas and Antoine Janis, who had each spent 52 years among the Sioux. Antoine LaJeunesse traded with the Utes and lived through a terrible winter.

A-C040.description: Mrs. Wheeler mentions near La Porte “Colona” or “Corona,” a Catholic mission to the Indians “long before Denver” (Colona is the old name of La Porte). This Cache la Poudre settlement was founded by French-Canadian trappers, including Antoine Janis.
A-C040.note: The “mission” character is reported by a single informant.

A-C056.description: Louis Vasquez, son of Benito Vasquez of St. Louis and Julie Papin, is Jim Bridger's partner at Fort Bridger. His son Hiram, abducted as a child by a young Shoshone and adopted for a time in Washakie's band, is found in Great Salt Lake City. Around 1852, Vasquez returns to Missouri, passing by the great treaty council of 1851.

A-C061.description: Pierre Lesperance founds the plaza of Los Valles de San Gerónimo, at the head of the Tecolote, and builds there the first sash sawmill in the region; his nephew, also named Pierre, later builds a circular saw there. A giant of about six feet, he could lift by himself a trough that twelve workmen did not dare move. According to Fred Desmarais, he died a few months after Pope Pius IX (1878). Maurice LeDuc lived for a time in the same village with a Sioux wife.

A-C062.description: Pierre Lesperance tells Octave Geoffrion about the death of La Ramée. A small band of trappers was trapping on the river now called the Laramie. One night Lesperance, who shared the same buffalo robe as La Ramée, was awakened by a death rattle: an Indian had just run his companion through with a lance. Lesperance knocked him down with his rifle, then the survivors spent the night barefoot in the snow on top of a hill. They lost their horses and equipment and walked two days without food before finding the main camp.
A-C062.note: Exact place unknown, somewhere on the Laramie River; traditional date around 1820-1821.

A-C063.description: On February 13, 1908, in Las Vegas, Cragin interviews Felipe Ledoux, son of Abraham Ledoux. Abraham and Antoine Ledoux, brothers from “the center of Canada,” arrived very early in New Mexico. Antoine had a son, José, who gave his name to the village of Ledoux, as well as a Métis son, Antoine, French-Pawnee, who lived for a long time at Fort Laramie. Felipe, born in Taos to a mother from the wealthy Trujillo family of Mora, took part in the Marcy-Loring expedition of 1858.

A-C066.description: In 1844 and 1845, Metcalf, the first husband of Mrs. Felipe Ledoux, trades at the Manitou soda springs, exchanging whiskey and coffee for buffalo robes with the Cheyenne and the Arapaho.

A-C067.description: In 1844 or 1845, at the Placita de Peñasco Amarilla (Hardscrabble), the French and the Americans give a great feast for the Utes, with bread and buffalo meat boiled with corn. It was also at the Hardscrabble plaza that Whittlesey killed Lafontaine and a Mexican woman named Candelaria, before fleeing to Fort El Pueblo.

A-C069.description: Francisco Trujillo, first husband of Maria Natividad Sandoval, is killed by Utes near Fort Uncompahgre, where he worked for Robidoux: sent to check the traps in the river, he is shot from the top of a hill. His widow then married old Istuss, a very brave trapper who had arrived early in New Mexico.

A-C086.nom: Chouteau's Island (Arkansas): Pawnee, Cheyenne — Old Bark
A-C086.description: Chouteau's Island, on the Arkansas, owes its name to the fight sustained in 1816 by Auguste-Pierre Chouteau and Jules De Mun against the Pawnee. Jesse Nelson places there, in 1857, a tense encounter between Kit Carson and some Cheyenne, defused by the son of Chief Old Bark.

A-C087.description: According to Charles St. Vrain (Sopris, May 29, 1908), the children of Marcellin St. Vrain and Red, a Sioux woman, were born at Fort St. Vrain: Felix on June 17, 1842, Charles on October 17, 1844, and Mary on March 9, 1848. Ill, Marcellin left his family at the fort and went to be treated in a St. Louis sanatorium at his brothers' expense. Charles remembers the gate kept shut and an Indian woman hanged outside the walls.

A-C095.description: Antoine Leroux's mother dies in St. Louis around July 15, 1858. His sisters Elena and Marie lived there, married with families. Pablita believes that Wilson Primm, of St. Louis, was Antoine's first cousin. According to a family tradition, Leroux descended from a St. Louis trader who had ransomed from the Comanche the captive wife of Vialpando, of Taos.

A-C100.description: In the spring of 1856, Charles Autobees sets out from his Huerfano plaza for Bijou Basin to trade flour and corn with the Arapaho and the Cheyenne. Attacked opposite Avondale by 27 Utes under Kaneatch, the convoy fights from 10 a.m. until nightfall near Chico Creek. Siccamo, Autobees's Arapaho wife, fights bravely; Autobees is wounded in the arm. Seven Utes are killed, Kaneatch is wounded and the attack ends.

A-C107.description: According to Escalante's Carta (1778), cited by Erebio Chacon, a Frenchman arrived in New Mexico in 1719 and was the first to make known to the Spanish the name of the “Pananas” (Pawnee).

A-C110.description: Rafael Chacon describes the two forts of Bent, St. Vrain & Co. on the Canadian, which traded with the Kiowa, the Comanche and the “Montaneses” Apache. The older one was of logs and had disappeared by 1856-1858. The adobe one had walls a yard thick and 18 to 20 feet high, four corner towers and an entrance on the south.
